These previous studies have shown good agreement between simulated and measured yields in experiments conducted across wide range of biophysical environments where nutrient limitations and yield-reducing factors were effectively removed. The water-limited yield potential was simulated based on local measured weather, soil, and management practices and assumed no nutrient limitation and complete absence of yield-reducing factors such as weeds, pathogens, and insect pests. For each specific trial, we assessed changes in simulated water-limited yield potential over time for a fixed cultivar and set of management practices so that trends in simulated yield are solely attributable to weather variation during the specific time frame of each experiment (Supplementary Fig. 2). Since there were no statistically significant long-term trends in simulated yield potential (P > 0.363), we analyzed the yield data without any normalization by weather or simulated yields.

Available phenotypic yield data for the statistical analysis consisted of either variety means (UK dataset and 11 out of 130 trial-location-year combinations in Argentina) or raw data per plot (datasets from France and US and 119 out of 130 trials location-year combinations in Argentina) per individual trial. For trials for which raw data were available, weighted variety means were calculated using best linear unbiased estimates (BLUEs) derived from linear mixed models:

yin = μ + Gi + Rn + εin (1)

where yin is the phenotypic observation of genotype i in replicate n; μ is the trial mean; Gi is the fixed additive effect of the genotype i; Rn is the random effect of the replicate n and is ~N(0, σ2r); and εin is a random residual term attributable to the effect of the within-trial experimental error and is μ~N(0, σ2e). Models were fitted using REML59, as implemented in the “asreml” package60 for R61. Four datasets consisting of either variety means per trial (UK), variety BLUEs per trial (France and US), or both (Argentina), were used to (i) test the effect of the fungicide treatment on grain yield; (ii) estimate overall, genetic, and non-genetic linear trends for grain yield over the years covered by the trials; and (iii) compute the BLUEs of the individual variety effects per calendar year for fungicide-treated and untreated crops. We used the following linear mixed models to analyze the effect of fungicide in the four METs:

yijkm = μ + Fj + Yk + Ekm + Gi + (GY)ik + εijkm (2)

where yijkm is the phenotypic observation of genotype i in trial m, conducted in year k under the fungicide treatment j; μ is the overall mean; Fj is the fixed additive effect of the fungicide treatment j; Yk is the random additive effect of the year k and is ~N(0, σ2y); Ekm is the random effect of the trial m nested within year k and is ~N(0, σ2e); Gi is the random additive effect of the genotype i and is ~N(0, σ2g); (GY)ik is the random effect of the interaction between genotype i and year k and is ~N(0, σ2gy); and εijkm is a random residual term attributable to the combined effect of the within-trial experimental error and the genotype × trial (nested within year) interaction and is ~N(0, σ2e). The BLUEs of fungicide effects were computed from this analysis.

With the aim of estimating unbiased genetic and non-genetic progresses for grain yield23,24 over the years comprised by the MET datasets, our model incorporated a fixed genetic trend (β) with respect to the year of first testing of genotype i (ri) and a fixed non-genetic trend (γ) respect to the trial year k (tk) scaled to the first year (2002 in Argentina; 2004 in UK, 2000 in US; and 2001 in France) as follows:

yikm = μ + γtk + Yk + Ekm + βri + Gi + εikm (3)

where Yk and Ekm are the random environmental deviations from the non-genetic trend due to the effects of the year and trial nested within year, respectively; Gi is the random genotypic deviation from the genetic trend, and εijkm is a random residual term attributable to the combined effect of the within-trial experimental error and the genotype × year and genotype × trial (nested within year) interactions. All random terms in model (3) were assumed to follow a normal distribution. This linear mixed model was used to analyze breakouts from the MET datasets, stratified by the presence or absence of fungicide treatments. In a complementary analysis, the term βri was removed from the model to estimate the overall, i.e., genetic + non-genetic, yield trend for the undivided MET dataset. Finally, we computed the BLUEs of the individual variety effects per trial-year. To do so, we used the following linear mixed model for the analysis of the fungicide-treated and untreated crops in the four MET datasets:

yikm = μ + Gi + Yk + Ekm + (GY)ik + εikm (4)

The BLUEs of the variety × year effects were computed from this analysis.

## Paper

## Abstract

Studies that quantify the contribution of genetic improvement to crop yields typically rely on comparisons of old cultivars grown side-by-side with more recent ones. This approach, however, does not allow to distinguish gains in yield potential versus maintenance breeding that aims to keep cultivars adapted to the evolving biophysical environment, including pests, diseases, and climate. Here we show an overall wheat yield improvement of 73 kg ha-1 y-1 based on direct comparison of modern cultivars against older ‘check’ cultivars using data from multi-environment trials from Argentina, France, United Kingdom, and United States. However, almost half of this improvement (33 kg ha-1 y-1) is attributable to maintenance breeding needed to counteract the yield erosion of older cultivars, and the other portion (40 kg ha-1 y-1) can be associated with the higher yield potential of modern cultivars. We conclude that comparison of new versus old cultivars under current conditions leads to an overestimation of genetic gains in yield potential.

---

## Introduction

Yield potential is defined as the yield of a well-adapted cultivar when grown without water and nutrient limitations and with weeds, diseases, and insect pests effectively controlled1,2. Under these conditions, yield potential is determined by solar radiation, temperature, and atmospheric carbon dioxide concentration. In the case of rainfed crops, water supply and soil water storage impose another limit to yield potential3. Hence, in absence of climatic trends, changes in yield potential over time can be attributed to genetic traits influencing light interception and conversion to biomass as governed by photosynthesis, respiration, water-use efficiency, and biomass partitioning to grain4,5. Continuous gains in yield potential through genetic improvement is crucial to avoid yield plateaus and reduce land requirements for adequate crop production6–9.

Field studies quantifying genetic yield improvement often rely on side-by-side comparison of sets of historical cultivars in today’s environment10–19. In these studies, the slope of the linear regression between measured grain yields versus each cultivar’s year of release is assumed to represent the annual rate of yield potential gain due to genetic improvement. Other approaches to quantify genetic yield improvement consist of comparison of new cultivars against check cultivars during several years20 or analysis of large long-term variety multi-environment trials (MET) using mixed linear models21,22. A common assumption of the first two approaches (i.e., side-by-side testing of historical series and comparison between new and check cultivars) is that the yield of the check cultivars does not erode over time or that the yield erosion can be fully avoided with check replacement and/or management so that the measured genetic gain can be fully attributable to higher yield potential in newer cultivars23–25. This assumption can be criticized because it ignores the yield decline that occurs over time when cultivars lose adaptation to the evolving climate, atmospheric composition, soil properties, crop management practices, pest and disease pressure, hereafter referred to as a ‘yield erosion’7,26–31. Retrospective analysis of MET datasets allows counteracting this drawback as each cultivar was tested at their peak of use31. Consequently, observed yield differences between new and old cultivars at any point in time can be associated with (i) higher genetically determined yield potential in new cultivars, (ii) yield erosion of old cultivars, or (iii) a combination of both (Fig. 1). Both breeding to counteract yield erosion by maintaining cultivars adapted to the changing abiotic and biotic environments (maintenance breeding) or improving yield potential in new cultivars are useful and needed. However, many studies of this kind on major food crops have assumed that yield differences between old and new cultivars are solely due to genetic gain in yield potential without assessing the contribution from maintenance breeding.

Continued yield gains are essential to ensure adequate food supply while substantially reducing land conversion and greenhouse gas emissions due to expansion of crop production area6,32–34. Clarity on the factors with greatest contribution to yield advance in recent decades is essential for effective prioritization of future research to improve yields. In the world’s most productive cropping systems, increase in yield potential via genetic improvement is the trait that is most widely credited with greatest impact on yield trend in farmer’s fields35–37. But what if existing estimations of genetic gains in yield potential are wrong? Here, we distinguish maintenance breeding from gains in yield potential using wheat as a case study, which is the most widely grown staple food crop worldwide, with a global harvested area of 217 million hectares, which accounts for about one quarter of global cereal production and ca. 20% of human calories and protein38.

---

## Results

Yield trends over time
We assembled a database (post-2000) that consisted of multi-environmental trials (METs) in Argentina, United States (US), United Kingdom (UK), and France (Supplementary Fig. 1) evaluating 849 cultivars across 17 locations, and including 10 check cultivars that were released no more than five years prior to being included in a trial (to avoid missing any early and quick yield decay) and were tested thereafter against more recently released cultivars for a minimum of 10 years to capture any measurable yield decay over time. In addition, because high-yielding wheat stands have lush leaf canopies that are conducive to development of fungal diseases39,40, yield loss from these diseases was minimized by prophylactic, in-season applications of foliar fungicide across all cultivars in every trial. Most trials included separate treatments with and without fungicide across all cultivars (Supplementary Tables 1 and 2). Overall, our database included 13,003 cultivar×site×fungicide combinations x year combinations.

Average yield of top yielding cultivars and check cultivars oscillated over time due to inter-annual variation in weather conditions (Fig. 2). However, we could not detect any long-term climatic trend based on trends in simulated yields using process-based crop models and local measured weather (Supplementary Fig. 2). On the other hand, two distinct features were apparent from the observed trends in measured yields (Figs. 2 and 3). First, the yield difference between top yielding cultivars and check cultivars was negligible at the beginning of the time series (141 kg ha−1), indicating that the check cultivars chosen in our study were among the top yielding cultivars at the beginning of the trials. Second, the yield difference between the top yielding cultivars and check cultivars, based on fungicide-treated crops, increased over time at an overall rate of +73 kg ha−1 y−1, highlighting the contribution of breeding to crop yield improvement.

Distinguishing gains in yield potential versus maintenance breeding
At question is how much of the overall yield difference can be attributed to increase in yield potential versus maintenance breeding aiming to keep cultivars adapted to the evolving environment. To distinguish between these two components, we evaluated the overall yield trends of top cultivars and check cultivars in crops treated with foliar fungicide (Figs. 2 and 3). We found that maintenance breeding and yield potential gain have contributed similarly, given the observed rates of -33 kg ha−1 y−1 for checks and +40 kg ha−1 y−1 in top cultivars. Thus, ignoring the contribution of maintenance breeding, as done in previous studies, can lead to a substantial overestimation in yield potential gain. Additionally, untreated check cultivars showed larger yield reductions (-64 kg ha−1 y−1) than treated ones over time, suggesting an increased susceptibility to foliar diseases over time and, thus, a larger yet masked yield erosion.

We further investigated yield trends using the entire database (13,003 yield entries combining site, cultivar, year, and fungicide application) with a mixed-effects model analysis (Table 1). There was a substantial effect of fungicide in all four countries, with an average yield response of +1285 kg ha−1, which is equivalent to 20% of the yield of the untreated crop. Thus, we evaluated yield trends for treated and untreated crops separately and found that genetic gains in treated crops ranged from +32 to 62 kg ha−1 y−1 (0.5–0.9% y−1) across countries. On the other hand, a negative non-genetic trend, which is associated with yield erosion and counteracted by maintenance breeding, was apparent in all cases, except for fungicide-treated crops in UK, ranging from -33 kg ha−1 y−1 (US) to -137 kg ha−1 y−1 (France) in treated crops and from -72 kg ha−1 y−1 (US) to -229 kg ha−1 y−1 (UK) in untreated crops. These results were consistent with the trends shown in Figs. 2 and 3.

## Methods

Data from variety trials
We retrieved yield data from four METs in Argentina, France, UK, and US (Supplementary Fig. 1, Supplementary Tables 1 and 2). These trials assess the agronomic value of crops, including yield and diseases resistance in different environmental conditions. Collectively, the four countries where METs were located include 30 Mha and produce 129 Mtons of wheat, accounting for 14% and 17% of wheat global area and production, respectively (average from 2019–2021)38. We only included trial that complied with the following criteria: (i) replicated multi-year field trials including at least 10 years of data, (ii) conducted after 2000 and including semi-dwarf cultivars, (iii) located within main wheat producing regions in each country/region, (iv) included widely sown cultivars and (v) included ‘check’ cultivars that remained in the trials over a longer period of time compared with others (>10 years) and were incorporated to the trials within three years after their commercial release.

Following the above criteria, we compiled data from 17 replicated trial locations (Supplementary Fig. 1, Supplementary Table 1 and 2). All trials were rainfed and most of them have a treatment without fungicide and another that received at least one in-season foliar fungicide application. Inclusion of fungicide-treated and untreated crops allowed us to assess changes in crop susceptibility to diseases over time. There was a total of ten check cultivars across the 17 trial locations, which corresponded to cultivars that were widely grown across millions of hectares globally soon after their time of release. Overall, our database included 13,003 cultivar×site×fungicide×year combinations across four countries. On average, 31 cultivars were tested every year in each trial, ranging from 16 to 55 across trial-year observations. Our database size is reasonable and comparable to previous studies assessing genetic gains22–25,48.

Seed was regenerated every year for the check cultivars. Plot size ranged between 7 and 15 m2 (Argentina: 1.5×5 m; US: 1.5×10 m; UK: 1.65×9 m; France: 7–10 m2), which is a common size for variety trials. Crops received recommended management practices regarding sowing date, seeding rate, fertilization, and weed and pest management at each site every year. As a result, high yields were obtained in these experiments, which were, on average, 18% (US), 29% (Europe) and 45% (Argentina) higher than average farmer yields during the same period38. Likewise, except for US, average yields of the top performers were ±15% of the simulated yield potential in each region.

Data analysis
We excluded cultivar-year combinations with suspicious values (e.g., CV > 30% among replicates) and specific years with near crop failure due to drought, severe lodging, and/or frost as reported by local experts. A total of 1% cultivar-year observations were eliminated following our quality control. Subsequently, we calculated the average yield of the 10 top-yielding cultivars for each trial-year combination, excluding the checks. Such an approach helped us discard experimental and/or underperforming cultivars. We assumed that the average yield of the 10 top yielding cultivars in each year represented the yield potential and then evaluated yield trends of these highest yielders over time as a measure of changes in yield potential.

We assessed the influence of weather on the yield trends of both the top yielding and check cultivars. To do this, we retrieved the simulated water-limited yield potential associated to the closest location to each trial available at the Global Yield Gap Atlas (www.yieldgap.org). Water-limited yield potential is determined by solar radiation, temperature, CO2 concentration, precipitation, and soil properties influencing the water balance1. Briefly, the water-limited yield potential was estimated using process-based crop models including CERES-Wheat (Argentina), SSM (US), and WOFOST (France and UK)52–54 that were specifically validated to be used in the target sites55–58. These previous studies have shown good agreement between simulated and measured yields in experiments conducted across wide range of biophysical environments where nutrient limitations and yield-reducing factors were effectively removed. The water-limited yield potential was simulated based on local measured weather, soil, and management practices and assumed no nutrient limitation and complete absence of yield-reducing factors such as weeds, pathogens, and insect pests. For each specific trial, we assessed changes in simulated water-limited yield potential over time for a fixed cultivar and set of management practices so that trends in simulated yield are solely attributable to weather variation during the specific time frame of each experiment (Supplementary Fig. 2). Since there were no statistically significant long-term trends in simulated yield potential (P > 0.363), we analyzed the yield data without any normalization by weather or simulated yields.

Available phenotypic yield data for the statistical analysis consisted of either variety means (UK dataset and 11 out of 130 trial-location-year combinations in Argentina) or raw data per plot (datasets from France and US and 119 out of 130 trials location-year combinations in Argentina) per individual trial. For trials for which raw data were available, weighted variety means were calculated using best linear unbiased estimates (BLUEs) derived from linear mixed models:

yin = μ + Gi + Rn + εin (1)

where yin is the phenotypic observation of genotype i in replicate n; μ is the trial mean; Gi is the fixed additive effect of the genotype i; Rn is the random effect of the replicate n and is ~N(0, σ2r); and εin is a random residual term attributable to the effect of the within-trial experimental error and is μ~N(0, σ2e). Models were fitted using REML59, as implemented in the “asreml” package60 for R61. Four datasets consisting of either variety means per trial (UK), variety BLUEs per trial (France and US), or both (Argentina), were used to (i) test the effect of the fungicide treatment on grain yield; (ii) estimate overall, genetic, and non-genetic linear trends for grain yield over the years covered by the trials; and (iii) compute the BLUEs of the individual variety effects per calendar year for fungicide-treated and untreated crops. We used the following linear mixed models to analyze the effect of fungicide in the four METs:

yijkm = μ + Fj + Yk + Ekm + Gi + (GY)ik + εijkm (2)

where yijkm is the phenotypic observation of genotype i in trial m, conducted in year k under the fungicide treatment j; μ is the overall mean; Fj is the fixed additive effect of the fungicide treatment j; Yk is the random additive effect of the year k and is ~N(0, σ2y); Ekm is the random effect of the trial m nested within year k and is ~N(0, σ2e); Gi is the random additive effect of the genotype i and is ~N(0, σ2g); (GY)ik is the random effect of the interaction between genotype i and year k and is ~N(0, σ2gy); and εijkm is a random residual term attributable to the combined effect of the within-trial experimental error and the genotype × trial (nested within year) interaction and is ~N(0, σ2e). The BLUEs of fungicide effects were computed from this analysis.

With the aim of estimating unbiased genetic and non-genetic progresses for grain yield23,24 over the years comprised by the MET datasets, our model incorporated a fixed genetic trend (β) with respect to the year of first testing of genotype i (ri) and a fixed non-genetic trend (γ) respect to the trial year k (tk) scaled to the first year (2002 in Argentina; 2004 in UK, 2000 in US; and 2001 in France) as follows:

yikm = μ + γtk + Yk + Ekm + βri + Gi + εikm (3)

where Yk and Ekm are the random environmental deviations from the non-genetic trend due to the effects of the year and trial nested within year, respectively; Gi is the random genotypic deviation from the genetic trend, and εijkm is a random residual term attributable to the combined effect of the within-trial experimental error and the genotype × year and genotype × trial (nested within year) interactions. All random terms in model (3) were assumed to follow a normal distribution. This linear mixed model was used to analyze breakouts from the MET datasets, stratified by the presence or absence of fungicide treatments. In a complementary analysis, the term βri was removed from the model to estimate the overall, i.e., genetic + non-genetic, yield trend for the undivided MET dataset. Finally, we computed the BLUEs of the individual variety effects per trial-year. To do so, we used the following linear mixed model for the analysis of the fungicide-treated and untreated crops in the four MET datasets:

yikm = μ + Gi + Yk + Ekm + (GY)ik + εikm (4)

The BLUEs of the variety × year effects were computed from this analysis.

Comments from Reviewer #2:
This paper addresses the important problem of assessing long-term genetic trend in crop
breeding. The authors propose a method that they claim allows separating out effects of
maintenance breeding and gains in yield potential.
The method the authors use is based on a lot of ad hoc assumptions, and there is no discernible
underlying statistical model. The authors use moving averaged and simple linear regressions in
several places, but this does not amount to an explicit statement of an overall statistical model.
Response: Based on the comments made by Reviewer #2 (and other reviewers), we have re-
analyzed the dataset and grouped check cultivars by country, making the analysis more robust
and including multiple checks instead of a single one. We have added a new Figure 3, revised
Table 1, and modified associated text accordingly.
The authors assume that the average yield of the ten top yielding cultivars in each year
represents the yield potential. This ad hoc definition violates their own definition in line 49 as
“yield of a well-adapted cultivar when grown without water and nutrient limitations and with
weeds, diseases, and insect pests effectively controlled.” Under any real circumstances, there
are always nutrient limitations. In addition, observed yield is subject to substantial experimental
error, so assuming that observed yield = potential yield is quite heroic.
Response: Valid point. We note that, except for experiments in the USA, the yield of top-
performing cultivars are within 15% of the simulated yield potential and follow its inter-annual
variation. More pragmatically, we do not see a better way to test our hypothesis as data from
variety trials that were explicitly managed to achieve yield potential do not exist. Based on this
comment, we elaborated on this limitation in the Discussion section (L. 231-239 of revised MS).
Two assumptions seem particularly intriguing. (i) In line 292: “For one case with positive yield
trends in checks (Claire), we assumed that all genetic yield improvement corresponded to yield
potential gain.” No justification is given for this assumption. Also, making such an assumption
based on a single check and using this to assess trend would seem to make the approach quite
sensitive to misspecifications. (ii) In line 294: “Conversely, for two cases with negative trends in
top cultivars (…) we assumed that all genetic yield improvement corresponded to maintenance
breeding.” Again, this seems a very ad hoc assumption, and no justification is given.
Response: We admit that the text explaining the assumption was confusing. Briefly, if the yield
trend of top cultivars does not increase over time, it suggests a lack of genetic gain. In such
cases, and in absence of any climate trend, we assume that the yield difference between top
5
and check cultivars can be fully attributed to the yield erosion of the check cultivars. In our new
analysis, this is only applicable to UK. Based on this comment, we rephrased the text in the
caption to Table 1 caption and in the M&M section (L 329-330 of revised MS).
The authors seek to address the problem of yield decay of check cultivars. A paper that has a lot
to say on this problem is this:
Raymond et al. (2023)
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fcr.2023.109086

Comments from Reviewer #3:
The manuscript titled ‘Maintenance breeding and breeding for yield potential equally contribute
to genetic improvement in wheat yield’ by Andrade et al. has the goal to disentangle and
independently estimate the genetic gains due to what the authors call maintenance breeding or
breeding to offset genetic erosion due to adaptation to a changing biophysical environment (i.e.
changes in pests, diseases, and climate change), from contributions to an increase in yield
potential or the genetic gains associated to carbon assimilation and partitioning.
The idea behind finding a way to independently assess maintenance from yield potential
improvements is enticing and the authors make a good argument for the need and interest in
estimating them independently. The authors are on the right track on how to estimate those,
but the manuscript could be improved to provide stronger inference. There are some limitations
in the study that compromise the inference, including that the dataset is small and limited, the
estimation of the yield potential needs further explanation, and the actual statistical methods
used seems under-powered.
Response: Thanks for the comments. Please find below our detailed responses.
Dataset limitation. The main limitation of the dataset is its size. There are very few genotypes
used in each one of the sites with around 23-47 genotypes tested each year, there are few
checks, and even less sites. These are all quite small numbers for the broad inference that is
discussed in the manuscript. Furthermore, the dataset has an important confounding effect of
site and check-genotype. For example, based on Figure 2 and Supplementary Table S2, genotype
Baguette 10, SY200, and Claire were evaluated in a single site. There are 17 site-check
combinations and 15 total sites. This creates an inference problem; can the results be
interpreted beyond the check-site combinations? Would different conclusions have been
reached if the check had been tested in multiple sites? The check genotype Claire, for example,
6
is one of the checks that shows a negative grain yield erosion, or to say it in another way, grain
yield of Claire increases over time, and actual yields are well over the estimated yield potential
for the site. How can this be interpreted biologically? Had Claire been evaluated in multiple
sites; would the authors have gotten similar results? How can a yield above the yield potential
be explained? Maybe using larger datasets where check-genotypes are evaluated in multiple
environments and compared to larger genotypes could solve these limitations. Breeding-type of
dataset might be more appropriate for such a study as large datasets are generated.
Response: In response to this comment we have added data from another five extra long-term
experiments (one cultivar in Argentina x two fungicide combinations and three cultivar x site in
UK). Our database now includes 37 long-term experiments (cultivar × site × fungicide
combinations), each spanning 10+ years and evaluating 25–41 cultivars per year, across four
countries. Reviewer #3 may perceive a limitation in the number of check cultivars (originally
eight, now ten), but these were widely grown cultivars representing elite germplasm across
millions of hectares globally. Just for comparison, the recent study cited by reviewers #1 and #2
(Raymond et al., 2023) included six trials spanning 10 years each in one country. To summarize,
we believe our database size is reasonable and comparable to similar previous studies. In
response to this comment, we added text in the M&M section (L 273-277 of revised MS).
Yield potential estimations. The manuscript does not describe in great detail the methodology
used for yield potential. The issue discussed above with the check genotype Claire, where actual
yields were well above the yield potential seems like a problem. There seems to be a year with a
yield potential close to zero where actual yields were quite high (i.e. 12t, Figure 2). How can
those results be explained? In a broader and more conceptual way, the authors went into great
length to explain that there was a need to discriminate between maintenance breeding from
gains from yield potential. They go further to describe the yield potential as an environment
where genotypes are ‘grown without water and nutrient limitations and with weeds, diseases,
and insect pests effectively controlled’ (line 49-50). The manuscript uses a simulated water-
limited yield potential as a benchmark, using the Global Yield Gap Atlas, that has the issues
described above with Claire. In any case, the study does not seem to be posed to compare a
true yield potential given that the trials are rainfed and have other limitations beyond water (i.e.
management in cultivar evaluation trials is standard, but not optimal for every genotype. The
timing of disease management or fertilization as well as planting density and other
management practices may prevent a genotype from achieving its potential), and the water-
limited yield potential is used as a benchmark. How were these concerns addressed in the
current study?
added key references (L 300-316 of revised MS). Additionally, we discussed uncertainties and
limitations of crop models and experimental data in the discussion (L 226-250 of revised MS).
The fungicide vs no fungicide application comparison goes in the right direction of addressing
these, but does not yield the expected results. How can the results of environment degradation
be explained then?
Response: Yield erosion is an inclusive term that account for the yield decline that occurs over
time when cultivars lose adaption to the evolving climate, atmospheric composition, soil
properties, crop management practices, and pest and disease pressure, as reported in the
published literature (see cited refs in the MS). While we cannot conclusively determine the
exact cause(s) for wheat (and not the goal of our study), our MS makes a novel contribution by
demonstrating that it exists, even in the case of treated crops. We added a short sentence to
the discussion listing possible drivers for yield erosion (L 179-182 of revised MS).
Statistical analysis and power. After having a historical dataset, where the same check genotype
is used in all subsequent trials for a given site, the authors report a large year-to-year variability.
This variability is quite common in these types of experiments, creating genotype by year
interactions. The authors then use the average of the first three years in the series and compare
them to the last three years in the series (see Table 1 and Figure 3, materials and methods lines
287-291). This seems an odd choice for such an analysis. Why not use a regression over years if
the goal is to show the trend effects? It is clear that with the level of year-to-year variability,
finding significant differences will be a challenge for any statistical analysis, but a regression will
show a true trend compared to the arbitrary 3-years mean comparison choice. Furthermore, no
statistical significance is reported for this part of the manuscript. Are those effects significantly
different from zero? Finally, when a regression is used for trends, a regression on a three-year
moving average is used to smooth it out (Figure 4, materials and methods lines 302-308).
However, x values are no longer independent, and the p-values are therefore no longer valid. At
least not in a frequentist analysis, but the methods are not described in detail. Why not use the
regression on the original data? In a way it is also surprising that an alpha-value of 0.1 is used to
claim significance in the cases where a test was conducted. Given that less than 70g per year is
expected, the study seems quite under-powered to be able to reach these conclusions. Larger
datasets will be needed to find significant differences of that magnitude when year-to-year
variations are orders of magnitude different.
Response: Valid point. Based on this comment, we dropped the analysis based on a 3-year
moving average and instead run regression analysis with the annual observations. We have
added a new Figure 3, substantially revised Table 1, and modified the associated text. We also
included the SEM for each data observation across site-cultivar combinations every year.
Most of the papers described in the manuscript are not attempting to disentangle gains
associated to yield potential from maintenance breeding improvements, and although they may
have lost an opportunity, it does not mean they are wrong when claiming the total
genetic gains. The authors should check all their references to this topic and make their statements
unambiguous. For example, the title correctly states that both maintenance breeding as well as
improvements in yield potential are both contributors to genetic gain. For example lines 134-
135 and lines 204-210 seem to misrepresent other studies as not all studies claim to report
yield potential improvements, but mere grain yield gains.
Further characterization of the dataset would be useful. For example, genotypes with large
within trial variability were removed. Did specific genotypes always produce these issues, or
were those local problems due to single plot outliers? What was the heritability of the trials?
Further characterization of the top yields would also prove useful to the readers. Are there
significant differences between top yielders and the checks? Could the top yielders be further
characterized, including their distribution and/or range?
Response: These suggestions are well taken. However, they do not align with the specific goals
of our study so no change was made in the revised MS in response to this comment.
Finally, the authors rightly bring the concern over the tension between management and
breeding efforts, and the usefulness of a methodology such as this one to create awareness. We
agree that the concept is needed and well described in this manuscript, but a larger dataset and
improved statistical analysis will be needed. Additionally, the tension between management and
breeding can be bridged with further studies on the genotype by environment by management.
Response: Based on this comment, we have modified the statistical analysis (see previous
responses on this issue) and included two new check cultivars (from Argentina and UK).
